rv.q: Something Rotten! has established itself as Broadway’s funniest, splashiest, slap-happiest musical comedy in at least 400 years.
It's easily the funniest thing to arrive on Broadway since 'The Book of Mormon.'
Certainly the most fun of the spring musical openings on Broadway, "Something Rotten!" is a sharply directed piece that achieves a consistent world and never checks its own literacy.
This big, brassy musical comedy about two brothers trying to compete with Shakespeare is so funny and so smart that it almost makes up for the fact that it's not particularly original.
Nicholaw’s genius for reducing an audience to helpless giggles is on blazing display in Something Rotten!
Even if the show doesn’t finish as strongly as it starts, its giddy high spirits prevail.
Those looking for an antidote to the Tudor-era seriousness of Wolf Hall will find Something Rotten! seriously delightful.

Something Rotten! revels in its silliness while delivering such a nonstop blitzkrieg of production numbers, each out-doing the one before, that you hardly notice how much you've fallen in love with the Bottom bros...
This cheerfully anachronistic musical comedy about the invention of the musical comedy is a kaleidoscope of inside jokes, self-referential gags and winking tributes to the theater.
The show is exuberantly silly, and if you're in the mood for that brand of theatrical comfort food — a helping of song, dance and snark — 'Something Rotten!' delivers.
By the time this initially delightful, eventually repetitive Broadway extravaganza ends, you too may feel a slight impatience not only with Shakespeare but with the entire musical theatre genre.
The show's good-natured silly charms just feel hammered by an unrelenting tsunami of manic, frenetic, zanier-than-zaniest onslaught of collegiate show-biz humor.

It’s softly vulgar – there’s a near rhyme of “penis” and “genius”, to say nothing of those gluteal gyrations – but it settles for sweet when it ought to be scurrilous, comfortable when it ought to be really clever.
It is, quite simply, the best musical I have seen in ages, and producer Kevin McCollum has a hit on his hands.
"Something Rotten” is red meat for theatre lovers – it’s clever, bodaciously funny, ridiculously tuneful; and even if Act II feels a bit overdone, audiences are sure to eat it up.
Nothing stinks in Something Rotten!, a delightfully irreverent mash-up that should keep audiences laughing for years to come.
It’s rare that at least one of these gifted comedians isn’t on stage; when two or all three of them converge, it’s musical nirvana.
A high-spirited, gleefully acted, past-meets-present cultural mash-up, mixing high wit with low jokes.

A rare theatrical event…a wonderful musical farce. Anyone who wants to go to the theatre and have a great time, unburdened by a complicated plot, listen to fun lyrics, and experience two acts of non-stop laughter…this “very new musical” should be their play of choice!
Forsooth, we thinkest they will.
Even if you don’t get every allusion, the staging by choreographer and director Casey Nicholaw (“The Book of Mormon” and “Aladdin”) is consistently fun.
Even so, “Something Rotten!” is a great deal of cartoonish fun, especially for musical theater fans who can appreciate the inside references, which range from the megahit “Cats” to the flop “Chess.”
In a season awash with musicals that are either revivals or adaptations of movies, Something Rotten! is that something new we've all been looking for.
Go for the production numbers and the big-hearted turns from the leads, whose enthusiasm ultimately proves even more infectious than the plague.
Even if you haven't brushed up on your Shakespeare recently — or your musical theater — you'll find plenty that's amusing, if little that's memorable, in Something Rotten!
Something Rotten! is a very funny show indeed, and should please audiences although one wonders how non-theatre savvy houses will respond to all those musical comedy jokes.
It’s a part that Borle was born to play.
'Something Rotten!' has established itself as Broadway's funniest, splashiest, slap-happiest musical comedy in at least 400 years.
“Something Rotten” is just a pure delight.
SOMETHING ROTTEN! contains more laughs than all our other current Broadway shows combined.
This show is a riot and MUST SEE for musical theater fans

It’s a blissfully entertaining show that doesn’t pretend to contain anything particularly original, its premise being a reworking of films and shows like Amadeus and Shakespeare in Love, and its music paying homage to famed musicals like Gypsy, Fiddler on the Roof and Spring Awakening among others.

The first-act ensemble number “A Musical” — which crams in melodic and choreographic references to everything from All That Jazz to Evita to Rent to A Chorus Line, complete with Elizabethan-era-appropriate drawn headshots — takes a clever idea and piles on additional layers of hilarity.
Something Rotten!, a boisterous and jaunty ride not to be missed.
Something Rotten! is that rare piece of fluff that knows exactly where it stands while occasionally betraying an unexpected intelligence.
If nothing succeeds like excess, then the new musical “Something Rotten!” shapes up to be a howling Broadway smash at the St. James Theater.

A love of musicals is something of a requisite for enjoying Something Rotten, a crowd-pleasing new one that opened on Broadway last night at the St. James Theatre. An origin story in the form of a send-up, the comedy about the first ever musical packs enough references to the Broadway canon to give any theatre queen whiplash.
Casey Nicholaw pulls out every trick in the theatrical book to keep you from laughing so hard and smiling so much
A dream cast lands all the outrageous laughs in this delectably hilarious new musical.
Rotten this show is anything but.

cn.t: Critics find this Shakespeare-spoofing musical a crowd-pleasing, laugh-filled love letter to Broadway, though some note it prioritizes silly spectacle over substance. The showstopper "A Musical" and energetic performances earn widespread praise.

sg.ra: Rows B-L are the house's actual sweet-spot band — Row A loses legroom and cranes necks because the St. James stage is raised on multiple recent productions (Sunset's LED wall, Something Rotten!'s set), while Row L is the last row before both the shallow rake AND the mezzanine overhang bite into the view Rows M+ hit the St. James's signature rake-and-overhang double-whammy — shorter patrons report 'craning around heads' and top-of-stage cutoff; a below-average experience for a 1,710-seat house

The Row D aisle-angled seats (D1/D2) are a genuine St. James unicorn — the row is set at a different angle than the rows in front so no seat sits directly ahead of you; this bypasses the flat-rake problem that defines the rest of the house 'Partial view' labeled seats in rows A-C side orchestra are heavily production-dependent — Into The Woods and Sunset (downstage-centric) work fine; Frozen's left-side set wall and Something Rotten!'s spread staging defeat them Back rows Q-S side orchestra sit directly under the mezzanine overhang — OK view of downstage action but top-of-set elements (screens, signage) cut off

Front mezzanine (Row A) is frequently called the best seat in the 1,710-seat house — Wikipedia notes the mezz 'extends over what were originally the tenth row of orchestra seats,' so you're unusually close for an upper tier, and because the orchestra's rake is so shallow, veterans repeatedly prefer Row A mezz to mid-orchestra at this specific house Row A has two specific St. James quirks that are production-sensitive — a low brass railing and an extension lighting rig on the mezz front; fine for average height but shorter patrons hit them, and Sunset Boulevard's onstage-lip blocking can make Row A worse than Row B-C

Front rows A-C side mezzanine are the house's best discount — St. James veterans (Patash: 'Gypsy, Bullets Over Broadway, A Funny Thing Happened... my favorite seats... I don't mind the side section in the least') buy them deliberately over pricier orchestra for every major musical High-seat-number side mezz (>18 in rows B-F) hits the mezzanine curvature problem — not just off-angle but the row pitches away from the stage creating sub-inch knee clearance Row B seat 18 area (where pricing typically breaks to a cheaper bracket) is a genuine value sweet spot — view is nearly identical to Row A but noticeably cheaper; confirmed across multiple productions

Rear mezz is the house's classic value trap — priced as mezzanine but the rake flattens and you're a third of the way back in a 1,710-seat house; reviewers describe needing seat boosters and sliding to the seat edge to see anything. Row Q aisle has an additional specific quirk: a corridor-exit light stays on during the show. Row J is the one exception in the rear-mezz block — it's the first row of a rear bank with a walkway in front, so no heads block the view; veterans specifically target it as the discount version of front mezz

Row A center balcony is the upper-tier's saving grace — BWW veterans split sharply (one calls it 'one of the worst balconies on Broadway', others swear by it), but the consensus lands on Row A specifically because the no-lean position, sound improvement from the extra speaker truss, and low railing make it better than rear mezz for the same price The balcony is a physical climb — 'like climbing a tower' — and is the second balcony; older patrons or anyone with mobility should not attempt at this house specifically Row A is the ONLY row that reliably clears the railing — behind Row A the rail bisects the stage; chain-reaction lean-forward effect forces everyone below to follow suit

Side balcony behind Row A combines every St. James hazard in one seat — side-angle, railing blocking downstage, second-balcony height, tight legroom, and (per multiple patrons) lottery-only sales because the house knows they're problematic Row A side balcony aisle seats (1-3 L, 2-4 R) are the one exception — sightlines avoid the railing, you're 'almost right over the front of the mezzanine,' and legroom is usable; anything behind Row A or away from the aisle is genuinely skip-tier at this house because back side-balcony also carries sound-mix issues off-axis from the speaker truss
